# The Desktop: Keeping Secrets Out of the Browser

Desktop applications built on web technology run a browser engine inside a
native window. That gives them a rendering stack, a layout engine, and a
large ecosystem, and it also gives them a browser engine's attack surface:
cross-site scripting, supply-chain compromise of a JavaScript dependency,
and a memory model in which a string, once created, may be copied by the
garbage collector and linger long after it is "deleted." For a program whose
purpose is to show people their passwords, that is the wrong place to keep
anything.

The FOKS desktop is built with Tauri, a framework that pairs a system
WebKit or WebView2 renderer with a Rust host process. This chapter is about
the arrangement that keeps key material and file contents out of the
renderer, and about a handful of engineering ideas that recur throughout the
host: generation counters, time-of-check-to-time-of-use races, digest-only
tracking, and bounded background work.

## Three tiers

```
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
|  WebKit renderer (React, TypeScript)              UNTRUSTED     |
|  - sees one revealed value at a time, on request               |
|  - never sees file bytes, vault keys, or signing keys          |
|  - can call: three Tauri core commands + app commands          |
+------------------------------+--------------------------------+
                               | Tauri IPC (JSON)
+------------------------------v--------------------------------+
|  Rust host (foks-desktop, Tauri)                  PRIVILEGED    |
|  - owns the window, dialogs, clipboard, drag-and-drop          |
|  - enforces the app lock on every value-bearing command        |
|  - streams file bytes between disk and the agent               |
+------------------------------+--------------------------------+
                               | Unix domain socket (foks-rs.sock)
+------------------------------v--------------------------------+
|  foks-agent (separate process)                    HOLDS KEYS    |
|  - all cryptography, all network sessions, all databases       |
|  - also serves the CLI and the MCP server                      |
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
```

The renderer is treated as untrusted. It renders a catalog of names,
types, sizes, and whether each small file holds a login; it asks for one
value at a time; and it receives that value only through the single
content-returning command. The host is
privileged but holds no long-lived secrets: it forwards requests to the
agent and moves bytes between the agent and the disk or clipboard. The
agent, described in [Chapter 19](19-agent.qmd), is a separate process that
outlives the window and that the command-line tool and the MCP server
([Chapter 21](21-mcp.qmd)) connect to as well.

## Exactly three core permissions

Tauri's capability model is an allowlist: a JSON file names which of the
framework's built-in commands a window's scripts may invoke. The default
set, `core:default`, expands to 92 commands, including
`core:image|from_path` (read any file the renderer names) and
`internal_toggle_devtools`. The FOKS capability file grants three:

| Permission | What it allows |
|---|---|
| `core:event:allow-listen` | subscribe to events the host emits |
| `core:event:allow-unlisten` | unsubscribe |
| `core:window:allow-start-dragging` | drag the window by its custom title bar |

Notably absent are `emit` and `emit_to`: the renderer cannot synthesize
events, so it cannot fake a file drop. The bundled dialog and clipboard
plugins are linked but granted no renderer permissions; only Rust drives
them.

A permission file is easy to get subtly wrong, so the project checks it by
test rather than by inspection. At build time Tauri generates an ACL
manifest describing every permission set and the commands each resolves to.
A unit test parses that generated manifest and the generated capability,
resolves each granted permission recursively to concrete
`manifest|command` pairs, and asserts that the Tauri commands in the
resulting set are exactly the three listed above. It then asserts a list of forbidden commands
(`core:image|from_path`, `core:path|resolve`,
`core:webview|internal_toggle_devtools`, `core:event|emit`, and others) is
unreachable. The project's permission notes give the reason this matters:
whether a command is *compiled in* is not the security boundary, because
Cargo feature unification across a workspace can pull in features a
sibling build enabled; only the capability file is a control, and only a
test that resolves it proves what it grants.

Application-defined commands are covered too, but only because the app
declares an ACL manifest: without one, Tauri runs any registered command for
any window on the app's own origin. The desktop build script lists every
registered command, Tauri generates an allow permission for each, and the
same capability file grants those permissions to the main window only. The
hosted-admin windows, which load a server's admin page from a remote HTTPS
origin, match no capability and are refused every command before it runs.
Tests compare the build script's list, the capability and the handler
registration, and ask Tauri's runtime authority which windows and origins
may call each command. Every command still begins with its own check that
the call came from the main window, and every command that can return a
value also checks that the app is unlocked.

## The app lock: a generation counter

An *app lock* hides everything after a period of inactivity or on request,
and requires the person to authenticate before anything is shown again. The
subtle requirement is not the locking but what happens to work that was
already in flight. Suppose a multi-chunk download started, the app locked,
the person unlocked it, and the download's next chunk arrived. Is the app
unlocked? Yes. Should the download continue? No: the lock was meant to end
the session in which it was authorized.

A *generation counter* solves this. A monotonically increasing integer is
incremented on every lock; an operation records the generation when it
starts and, before doing anything sensitive, checks that the app is
unlocked *and* the generation is unchanged. A lock followed by an unlock
leaves the app unlocked but advances the generation, so the check fails.
The general pattern appears wherever "the same state" is not the same as
"a state that looks identical": caches invalidated by a version number,
optimistic concurrency by a version column, and so on.

In the host, `AppLock` holds a `locked` flag, a `generation` counter, and
an `authenticating` flag, all atomics. `lock()` sets the flag and
increments the generation. Long operations bracket themselves with two
calls:

```
g = unlocked_generation()          // read generation, require unlocked
... do work, possibly across many IPC round trips ...
require_unlocked_generation(g)     // require unlocked AND generation == g
```

A unit test named for the property, that locking invalidates work even
after unlock, pins it. The lock starts *engaged* on a platform that can
authenticate and *disengaged* on one that cannot, so the interface can
never become permanently inaccessible. Locking also scrubs: it invalidates
the cached catalog, closes any hosted-administration windows, and clears
delivered chat notifications. Unlocking uses `authenticating.swap(true)` so
a second prompt cannot open while one is pending.

### Delegating authentication to the operating system

FOKS has no master password. Authentication is delegated entirely to the
operating system, so the application never stores or compares a secret of
its own.

On macOS, the host asks `LAContext` whether biometric policy is available
(to label the mechanism "biometry" or "password") and then evaluates the
`DeviceOwnerAuthentication` policy, which accepts Touch ID, an Apple Watch,
or the account password. A 60-second timeout bounds the prompt, and the
three cancellation error codes (-2, -4, -9: user, system, and application
cancel) are reported as "not authenticated" rather than as failures.

On Linux, the host calls polkit over the system D-Bus. It first checks
that the action `com.aka.foks.desktop.unlock` is registered (the policy
file is installed by the package; if it is missing, the lock reports itself
unavailable rather than silently allowing). It then calls
`CheckAuthorization` with a *subject* of kind `unix-process` identified by
the host's PID and its **start time**, read as the 22nd field of
`/proc/<pid>/stat`. Including the start time matters because PIDs are
reused: a subject identified by PID alone could, after the original
process exits, name an unrelated process. The policy file sets
`allow_active=auth_self` and denies inactive and remote sessions, so only
the user at the active console can authenticate, and no administrator
privilege is involved.

## Time-of-check to time-of-use

A *TOCTOU* race is a bug in which a program checks a property of something
(a file, a process, a socket) and then acts on it, but the thing changes in
between. The check was correct when made and wrong when relied upon. The
defense is to make the check and the use atomic, or, when that is
impossible, to identify the thing by an unforgeable handle (an inode, a
process start time) and re-check that handle immediately before acting.

The host does this in several places. Before it launches the packaged
agent, it verifies the binary is a regular file (not a symlink), owned by
the same user as the desktop, not writable by group or world, and
executable. When it finds an incompatible agent already bound to the
socket, it reads the peer's PID from the socket (`LOCAL_PEERPID` on macOS,
`SO_PEERCRED` on Linux), shows the person a confirmation dialog naming
that process, and then **re-inspects the socket after the dialog closes**.
If the endpoint no longer matches what was shown, no signal is sent, since
approval applied only to the endpoint originally displayed. The polkit
start-time subject above is the same idea applied to processes.

## Clipboard hygiene

Copying a password to the clipboard hands it to every clipboard-history
tool on the machine. The host's `copy_with_hygiene` does three things:

1. It computes `SHA-256(value)` and a generation number, writes the value
   to the pasteboard, and then drops the zeroizing string. Only the 32-byte
   digest and the generation are kept in memory.
2. A thread sleeps for the auto-clear interval and then calls
   `clear_if_unchanged`: it reads the current clipboard text, hashes it,
   and clears the clipboard **only if the digest still matches**. A value
   the person copied in the meantime is never destroyed. The generation
   ensures a repeated copy of the same value gets its own timer.
3. On macOS it also sets the `org.nspasteboard.ConcealedType` pasteboard
   type, a convention that asks clipboard managers not to record the item.
   Linux has no equivalent, which is why its timer is shorter.

| Platform | Auto-clear |
|---|---|
| Linux | 15 s |
| macOS and others | 30 s |

The exit handler performs one best-effort clear before the process ends.

## Logins

FOKS v0.1.9 has no login type. The desktop stores a login as an ordinary
small file of UTF-8 `key: value` lines, `user: …`, `password: …` and
`url: …`, so Go clients read and write it as any other value.

The catalog marks which small files are logins without carrying their
contents. A metadata listing already fetches and opens every small-file
node to authenticate it. Before it zeroizes that plaintext, `foks-client`
records one bit, `shape: login` when the text has the layout the desktop
writes and `shape: other` otherwise, and the bit travels through
`KvCatalogReport`, the agent's `KvEntryMetadata` and its retained catalog
pages, and the host's `ItemDto`. It is agent IPC only and never reaches the
Go wire. The renderer lists a small file with `shape: login` as a Password
wherever it is filed; a catalog entry without a shape, from an agent that
predates the field, falls back to the `/logins/` folder. Such a Password
may hold no `password:` line, so its rows, its palette entry and its
details panel also offer Copy value.

Copy on a login reaches the clipboard one field at a time.
`copy_item_field` reads the exact listed version, selects the password,
user name or website line in the host, and passes only that value to
`copy_with_hygiene`; the other lines are dropped with the zeroizing read
buffer. Lines are separated by `\n` with one trailing `\r` removed. A field
line splits at its first `:`; its key is not trimmed and must be non-empty
with no ASCII whitespace, so an indented `  password: x`, a spaced
`password : x` and a sentence such as `Reset it at https://example.com` are
not field lines. Neither is a line whose `:` is followed directly by `//`,
such as a bare URL. The value loses exactly the one space the desktop
writes after the `:`, so a password that begins or ends with a space is
copied whole. `user` and `username` name the user name, `url` and `website`
name the website, and the first line naming a field wins. A small file is a
login when every line that is not blank is a field line and one has the key
`password`; an indented YAML document, an INI section, or a note with a
line of prose or a URL stays a Document with Copy value. A note line of the
form `Note: text` is a field line, so a login may carry it and the details
panel lists it as its own row. A field that is absent or empty
fails with `field-missing` instead of copying something else. Both the
listing's classification and the host's field selection use
`foks_client::kv::login`, so an item listed as a login has a password line
the host finds, though that line may be empty and then fails with
`field-missing`. The renderer's `model/login.ts` applies the same rules to
text it has read. `copy_item_value` copies a text document's whole value; it
is `copy_item_field` with the field `value`.

The ⌘K search palette copies through the same two commands: ⌘C on a
highlighted Password copies its password, ⇧⌘C its user name, and ⌘C on a
text document its value, so a value reaches the clipboard without being
shown or opened. The same keys do the same on the focused row of the Files
list. ⌘O on a highlighted Password calls `open_item_url`, which reads the
exact listed version, selects the website line as `copy_item_field` does,
and hands it to the platform's opener (`open` on macOS, `xdg-open` on Linux)
only when it is an http or https address with a host and no user name or
password; a value with no scheme, such as `example.com/login`, is taken as
https. The address is not returned to the renderer, and a lock that engages
during the read stops the browser from opening. A missing website fails with
`field-missing` and any other value with `website-unsupported`. The palette
searches names and paths only, never values.
Its Recent and Favorites lists are kept in the webview's local storage,
which is not cleared by the app lock, so they hold an item's `StoreRef` and
dirent id and nothing else. The `StoreRef` names the server profile, the
account and, for a team, the team's alias and id; item names and paths are
resolved from the snapshot while the app is unlocked. A dirent id names the
entry at one path: a move or a rename writes the item under a new dirent id
at its destination and leaves a tombstone with the old id, which an item
later created at that path reuses. The app follows a move it made to the new
id once the refreshed snapshot holds the item; after a move made elsewhere
the entry is no longer listed, until an item created at the old path takes
its place.

The New password sheet and the login Edit form give the password Show and
Generate. Generate draws a password in the renderer, which already holds
the typed password in both forms, so the plaintext reaches no process it
did not reach before. A random-character password is 8 to 64 characters
from the selected sets (upper case, lower case, digits and 13 symbols), by
default 24 characters from all four with `0 O 1 l I` left out. A passphrase
is 4 to 8 words, by default 5, from the BIP-39 English list the recovery
phrase input already embeds, joined by a hyphen, space, period or
underscore. Each character or word is an index drawn with
`crypto.getRandomValues` and rejection sampling, so it is uniform over its
pool, and the strength shown for a value taken from the generator is its
exact entropy, `length × log2(pool size)` bits: 147 bits for the default
password, 11 bits per word. A typed or stored password is not measured. It
is checked against a short list of common passwords (also with its
separators removed, so a well-known passphrase matches), the site's
registrable label (`slack` in `app.slack.com`, not the subdomain), the
user name and each part of it (`john` and `smith` in
`john.smith@example.org`), one unit of up to four characters repeated
(`aaaaaaaa`, `asdfasdf`), a run of consecutive letters or digits or of a
keyboard row (`abcdefgh`, `poiuytre`), also before a trailing run of
digits and symbols (`abcd1234!`), and the 8-character minimum. A match shows a
warning at the lowest level without disabling Create or Save; a value with
no match reads "Not measured · no common weakness found". The strength
text is a polite live region, so a warning is announced as it appears. The
candidate in the generator cannot be selected; Use password is the way to
take it. The generator's last settings, never a password, are kept on the
device under the `passwordGenerator` `localStorage` key. A generated
password is stored as any other `password:` line.

## Files: drag-and-drop, upload, and download

A web `<input type="file">` reads bytes into a JavaScript buffer. FOKS
wants uploads without bytes in the renderer, but it also must not turn a
"path-taking" command into a general file reader that the renderer could
point at any file on disk.

The drop event lands in Rust, because Tauri's `dragDropEnabled` routes it
to the host. `record_drop_paths` accepts **exactly one** UTF-8 path as
authorized; a multi-file drop is reported for display but authorizes
nothing. The renderer then calls `upload_path` with the path string it was
shown, and the host looks it up in the pending set: a path that was not
dropped, or was already consumed, yields `drop-not-authorized`. Paths
chosen through the native picker never cross the IPC boundary at all. The
host rejects symlinks and non-regular files, then streams the file to the
agent in frames of at most 700 KiB, the agent protocol's payload bound
from [Chapter 17](17-wire.qmd), each held in a zeroizing buffer. A transcript
test carries an 84 MiB sparse file through the backend and confirms it
travels only as bounded frames.

Download reverses the path with three properties: atomicity, integrity,
and no plaintext left behind on failure. The host opens the native save
dialog itself, creates a temporary file **in the destination's directory**
(so the final rename is on one filesystem), and streams chunks from the
agent, validating that each chunk's store, path, version, and offset match
the request and that the running total stays under the limit. Each chunk
buffer is zeroized after it is written. When the agent signals end of
file, the total length is compared to the item's authenticated size; a
mismatch is a `response-binding` error. Then `sync_all` flushes the file
and `persist` renames it into place, which POSIX guarantees is atomic. A
crash at any earlier point leaves a temporary file, never a partial file
under the chosen name.

| Bound | Value |
|---|---|
| Inline KV write threshold (above this, stream) | 128 KiB |
| Stream frame | 700 KiB |
| In-memory reveal | 16 MiB |
| Download | 1 GiB |

The repository's HTML guide states the download limit as 512 MB; the code
defines 1 GiB, and the code is authoritative.

## The agent's lifecycle

The host launches the packaged agent with `--request-timeout-seconds 60`
(the agent's default of 15 s is too short for a path that may raise a
blocking macOS Keychain prompt), with standard input closed and standard
output and error redirected to a 0600 log file. A reaper thread waits on
the child so its exit status is observed. Exit is a one-way state machine
in the close guard, `Idle → Decision → Stopping → Finalizing`, with `Failed`
and `ForceConfirmation` branches, and the desktop process ends only after
the agent's termination has been verified; the state cannot move backward
from `Finalizing`.

**Startup failures.** The host waits for a launched agent to bind its socket
for as long as the process is alive, up to 60 seconds: an initialized agent
reads its vault key from the system credential store before it binds, and
that read can wait on a prompt. A socket that is missing or refuses
connections is the expected state until then. Any other probe failure, such
as an unsafe socket or a failed Hello or status request, is reported as it is
once it has persisted for 5 seconds. An agent still running when the wait
ends is kept: the next attempt waits on it again rather than launching a
second agent against the same state, reports its exit if it has exited since,
and drops it once an agent answers. Restoration after an export, import or
relocation, and Restart service on the restoration-failed screen, start the
agent through the same path, so they also wait up to 60 seconds, report a
timeout as `agent-start-timeout`, and reuse a kept agent; they hold the
exclusive maintenance reservation while they wait.

The startup dialog always offers Try Again and names `agent.log`. It offers a
reset only when the launched agent was observed to exit before it answered,
not when it is still starting, answers with an error, could not be launched,
or lost supervision. Before offering the reset, the host inspects the state
root with credential-store interaction disabled, as automatic recovery does;
if the store is locked or denies access, the dialog offers Try Again only and
says to unlock it or allow access. The reset deletes nothing:
`quarantine_unreadable_state` moves every entry of the state root except its
lock files into a new private sibling directory, `<root>.reset-<unix
seconds>`, on the same file system, and leaves system credential-store
entries in place, so moving the entries back restores the previous state.

## The notification consumer

The chat view must discover new messages across every channel of every
team without flooding the agent, while the conversation the person is
looking at must never feel stale. The consumer that does this is a small
exercise in bounded background work.

**Round-robin from a persisted cursor.** Each pass walks the inbox snapshot
in two segments starting at `cursor % size`, so the walk resumes where the
last one stopped rather than restarting at channel zero and starving the
channels at the end. The walk allocates no channel array.

**Bounds and budgets.**

| Bound | Value |
|---|---|
| Queued jobs | 64 |
| Progress records (baselines) | 4,096 |
| Rows per pass | 400 |
| Bytes per pass | 4 MiB |
| Rows per channel read | 100 |
| Bytes per channel read | 1 MiB |
| Evictions per 5 s window | 64 |

When the progress table is full, the consumer evicts an idle record before
admitting a new channel, but caps evictions per 5-second window so that
rotation "must not become an endless baseline RPC loop." Before starting a
job it reserves a whole channel read against the pass budget; a budget
miss re-arms after a short yield.

**Geometric backoff, with one exception.** A channel whose pass found
nothing new doubles its interval from 5 s toward a ceiling of 60 s; a
pass that observed a newer sequence resets it to 5 s. The module
documentation is explicit about what this trades: on a degraded host, a
message in a quiet, unopened channel may be noticed up to 60 s after it
arrives rather than up to 5 s. No message is skipped; the backoff decides
when the read happens, not whether. **The channel whose thread is open
never backs off**: the due-time computation uses the base interval whenever
the channel is the presented one, whatever interval is stored. Opening a
channel that had backed off therefore makes it due at the base interval
immediately.

Timers are armed for the earliest computed deadline, or not at all if
nothing is due; other wake-ups come from inbox publications or admission
releases. Baselines are seeded from the inbox projection's own head when it
is not degraded, costing no request.

## History paging

Chat history is paged with an opaque `before` cursor: a history reply
carries `messages`, `before` (the cursor for older rows, or null), and the
integrity fields `missing_predecessors` and `gap` described in
[Chapter 16](16-chat.qmd). An incremental refresh asks for rows `after`
the newest sequence held; if the reply reports a gap, the view falls back
to a full first page and replaces what it held.

A *published-head gate* avoids a class of wasted requests. The inbox
snapshot carries a `head` sequence per channel, and the decoder enforces
that `cursor <= head` and that `degraded` is true exactly when they
differ. When a revision arrives for a reason other than a new message,
the tail read is skipped if the published head is not beyond the newest
held sequence, because the server would only confirm that nothing newer
exists.

The history cache is a least-recently-used map keyed by a binding of
store, channel, scope, generation, and authority, bounded at 16 channels,
1,000 rows, and 8 MiB. Reading an entry re-inserts it to refresh recency.
A binding whose authority or generation has changed is simply not
current, so a page fetched under an old role cannot be shown after the
role changes. The row and byte limits come from the shared
`chat-limits.json` of [Chapter 24](24-performance.qmd).

## Vault edits

Items and folders offer Rename or move within their current vault. The target
is an exact absolute path, chosen as a folder of the vault's tree and a name or
typed in full, and a live destination is never overwritten. A destination
folder that does not exist yet is created first with `MkdirKv` and `mkdir_p`,
the operation New folder uses. The selected source dirent identity and version
remain fixed across retries, so a newly created object at the same path cannot
satisfy an older selection.

Several items chosen together, or dragged onto a folder, move as separate
`MoveKv` mutations, one at a time; there is no batched form. The host retires
a store's catalog after every write and selects the item of the next request
in a catalog it has read, so the desktop reads the catalog of the store's
profile again before each item and sends the current version of the same
dirent; an item whose path now holds another dirent is not sent. Each item's
outcome is reported on its own.
A failure whose request certainly did not run, such as a refused admission
while another write held the mutation permit, can be retried; an ambiguous
one cannot, because the item may already have moved.

Text edits and picked or dropped file replacements preserve the selected
dirent identity and version too. The client validates them before uploading
content and on every namespace retry, so recreation cannot redirect an open
editor or file picker to a different entry.

### Copy to another vault

`MoveKv` relinks a dirent within one store, so an item cannot move to
another vault: its content is sealed under that store's keys. Copy to vault
writes a new item instead. `copy_item_to_store` names the source by store,
path, version and dirent, which the host checks against its catalog as it
does for an edit, and the target by store, path and roles. The host reads
the source through the agent and creates the copy with a `Create`
precondition and `mkdir_p`, so content never crosses into the renderer and
an occupied path is refused rather than overwritten.

A large file cannot be streamed from source to target. The agent admits a
streaming upload exclusively for its profile, and a chunk read of the same
profile waits for that admission, so reading the source while uploading
the copy would wait on itself until the deadline. The host therefore reads
every chunk first, with the same binding checks as a download, into an
unlinked temporary file. Each chunk is sealed with ChaCha20-Poly1305 under a
fresh key held only in memory, with the chunk's sequence number as its
nonce, so the disk never holds plaintext and a chunk altered or reordered
on disk fails the upload. The upload then reads the chunks back and opens
them one at a time. The temporary directory therefore needs free space for
the whole file, and where it is a tmpfs that space is memory; the host
compares the file's listed size with the free space before the first read
and refuses a copy that would not fit.

When the stores are on different servers, the host takes its mutation
reservation for the whole application rather than for one profile. An
ambiguous outcome then blocks every later change until a complete listing
of every profile, so the renderer refreshes all servers rather than the
source's. Moving the original is a separate `trash_item` after the copy
succeeds: two mutations on two stores have no common transaction, and a
failure of the second leaves a copy and an original rather than neither.

### Importing passwords

Neither FOKS v0.1.9 nor this implementation has a `foks kv export`, and an
account already used with the command line needs none: its items are on its
server and appear once the account is connected through Import from FOKS
CLI. Logins kept in another password manager arrive as a CSV export, which
`begin_password_import` reads in the host. The renderer receives an opaque
id, the file's name and the name and folder of each login; the file's path
and every user name, password, website and note stay in host memory, in
zeroizing buffers, until the import is committed or discarded, another file
replaces it, or the app locks.

Columns are found by their header, so the CSV exports of 1Password,
Bitwarden, KeePass, KeePassXC, LastPass and the browsers' password managers
need no format choice. A login's name is its title, else its website's host,
else its user name; a `/` or `%` in it is percent-encoded as the Files list
decodes it, and a second login with the same name in the same folder takes
a ` (2)` suffix. A folder or group column becomes folders below the chosen
destination, without the `Root` group KeePassXC writes in every row.

`commit_password_import` writes each login as one small file of `user:`,
`password:` and `url:` lines, followed by one `note:` line per line of its
notes. Every line is then a field line, so the agent's listing classifies
the item as a login and Copy finds its fields, while Go FOKS clients see an
ordinary small file. A login longer than 2,040 bytes is stored as a file and
listed as a Document. Each write carries a `Create` precondition, so an
occupied path is reported and left unchanged, and a login that failed or
whose outcome is unknown can be sent again without saving it twice. The
writes run one at a time under one mutation reservation; the first failure
other than an occupied path ends the run, and an unknown outcome requires a
refresh before the next write, as for any other mutation.

`export_logins` goes the other way, for one vault. It writes the column
layout of a Bitwarden export: a password's folder (relative to `/logins`
when it is below it, so an import into `/logins` restores it), its decoded
name, the three fields Copy finds, and its other lines as notes, with the
`note:` prefix the import adds removed. The host reads each password at the
version the catalog listed and writes the records to a temporary file next
to the destination, which replaces the destination only when every record
is written; a lock during the export stops it and removes the temporary
file. The file is plain text, like every password manager's CSV export, so
the sheet asks for the vault's name before the save dialog opens.

### Trash

Delete in the desktop moves an item, or a folder with everything in it,
into `/.trash` in the same vault, as one `MoveKv` namespace mutation: a
tombstone at the source and a dirent at the destination. Nothing is
destroyed, so Delete asks for no confirmation. The toast it shows offers
Undo for eight seconds, and ⌘Z does the same while it shows. A child that
another device adds to a folder while it is moved goes with the folder,
which a recursive delete could not promise. Several items moved to Trash
together are sent one at a time, as several items are moved. Their Undo
restores the entries one at a time in the same way, each to the path its
item had; an entry whose original path holds a new entry stays in Trash.

Dirent names are sealed under the key of the directory that holds them, so
one shared Trash folder would expose the names of owner-only items to
members. Each read role has its own folder, `/.trash/owner`,
`/.trash/admin` or `/.trash/member-<visibility>`, created with that read
role, and an entry keeps its own read and write roles when it moves in. An
entry, file or folder, is filed by the most restrictive read role on its
path: its own and that of every folder above it, ordered Owner, Admin, then
Member by visibility. A member-readable login inside an admin-only folder
therefore goes to `/.trash/admin`. Its entry name records the folder names
above it, which were sealed under the admin key, and members who could not
list that folder could not reach the login before it moved either. A
folder's children move with it and stay sealed under its key. When another
item already holds a role folder's name with other roles, the next free
`/.trash/<role-tag>.<n>` is used instead. In a team, `/.trash` itself is
readable and writable through the low-visibility Member key every team root
uses, so any member who can delete an item can add the role folder it
needs.

Only an owner can create `/.trash` at the top level, because team roots are
owner-writable. Until an owner has moved any item to Trash, a member who is
not an owner cannot move items there. When the roster shows that, or the
host's attempt to create `/.trash` is refused by role (`trash-unavailable`)
and the roster does not show this account as an owner, Delete opens the
permanent-delete confirmation for the item instead and says why. Any other
failure to create `/.trash`, such as an exhausted quota or expired
credentials, keeps its own code and is reported as it is.
`remove_item` removes an item outside Trash only on that explicit request,
and only for a file in a team whose fully read catalog has no `/.trash`;
folders can be deleted only through Trash. The team's Trash view states the
same.

An entry is named `<UTC yyyymmddThhmmss>~<original path>`, with `%`, `/`
and control characters percent-encoded, for example
`20261014T093012~%2Flogins%2Fgithub.com`. When that name would pass the
255-byte component limit, it is `<stamp>~#<hash>`, where the hash is the
first 16 bytes of the SHA-256 of the original path, and a small file named
`<that name>.origin` beside it holds the original path.

Each vault's tree ends with a Trash row. Its view lists the entries the
account can read, newest first, with where each was and when it was
deleted; for a hashed name it reads the `.origin` file once per version.
Trash is not part of the ordinary folders, All items or search. Restore
moves an entry back. A missing parent folder is created readable only under
the more restrictive of the entry's read role and its Trash folder's, which
was the most restrictive on the original path. When the original path is
taken, Restore offers to restore the entry as `<name> (restored)` beside
the item there and never replaces it. Delete permanently and Empty Trash
use `RemoveKv`, recursive for a folder, and the host refuses them outside
`/.trash` except as above. Their confirmation says what they cannot
promise: the server keeps every dirent version, so earlier encrypted
versions may remain on it.

Entries keep their own write roles in a role folder, so a member can list
an entry that only an admin can remove. Empty Trash removes the entries
this account can change and lists the ones that stay. It sends them to
`empty_trash` in one host mutation planned from one catalog read; removing
them one command at a time would fail after the first, because each write
discards the store's catalog items. `empty_trash` also removes `.origin`
files whose entry is gone, which a move into Trash that failed after
writing its `.origin` file leaves behind, but only when the store's catalog
was read completely. Removing a hashed entry's `.origin` file is the last
write of a restore or permanent removal, and its failure does not fail the
command: the entry has already moved, and an `.origin` file without its
entry is harmless.

Trash is emptied by hand unless a device opts in. Settings › Preferences ›
Trash can empty it automatically after 30 or 90 days, a choice kept in that
device's local storage. While the app runs, it removes the entries older
than that which this account can change, through `empty_trash`, one store
at a time and at most hourly per store. It starts only after the catalog has
been unchanged for three seconds, and not while a dialog is open, a Trash
action or an Undo runs, or an Undo is offered. A move to Trash or a restore
started while it runs waits for it instead of being refused for the host's
single mutation permit.

Go FOKS clients and the CLI list `.trash` as an ordinary folder. The layout
needs no protocol or storage change, and a Go client can restore an entry
with an ordinary move.

The card grid windows whole rows at the current viewport width through
`files-grid.ts`, so it can scroll through the full loaded catalog without
mounting every card. It no longer imposes the former 200-card cap.

## Reviewing exposure after a removal

Removing a member rotates the team's keys and lowering a role rotates the
keys of the roles the member loses, as [Chapter 15](15-teams.qmd) describes;
removing a device ends its access to the account. Each change stops later
reads only. A credential the party already read, such as an API token or a
Wi-Fi password, stays valid where it is used until it is changed there.

The Remove, Lower role, Remove federated team and Remove device sheets
therefore list, before the write, the items the party could read: for a
member or a federated team, the team's items whose read role its role
admits; for a lowered member, those the new role no longer admits; for a
device, every item in its account's own store and in the account's teams,
since the device held the account's keys. A team whose setup has not
completed is not included, since no device read its items. The list comes
from this account's catalog, so it is a lower bound: an item this account
cannot list, a Trash entry and a folder are not in it, and the sheet says so.
The sheet waits until the store's items, and for a member the roster, have
been read. If a member's team cannot be read, the change can still be made,
but no list is kept. A device's list leaves out only the stores whose items
could not be listed and names them.

Once the write reports success, or fails in a way that does not show whether
it was applied (the agent connection was lost, for example), the list is kept
on this device as a review; after such a failure the party may already be
gone from the roster or the device list, and the sheet could not be opened
for it again. A later change for the same party and team adds to that review;
an item listed again replaces its earlier entry and mark, since the party
could read it again. The team page or Devices shows a band until each entry
is marked Rotated or Not needed, and closing the review sheet with every
entry marked removes the review. The review sheet opens an item in Files,
where Edit can generate a new password. An entry whose item has a higher
version than at the change reads "Changed since removal" ("Changed since role
change" after a demotion): any write raises the version, so the user confirms
rotation rather than the app assuming it. An entry whose dirent id is no
longer listed, because the item was moved, renamed or removed, reads "Not
listed". If storage refuses a review, a notice says so.

Reviews are kept in the webview's local storage under
`foks.exposureReviews`, which persists while the app is locked. A review holds
`StoreRef`s, dirent ids, versions and marks, the removed party's id, and its
username or device name, which the server also holds; it holds no item name
or path, which the sheet resolves from the live snapshot. The review needs
no agent operation and no protocol change.
